food.text: In the British Isles and northern France the climate was generally too harsh for growing grapes and olives. Beer became the commoner's drink in the north, while wine was an expensive import.

After Roman rule ended in Britain and the Western Roman Empire collapsed, the use of more exotic food items lessened. British cooking then consisted mostly of vegetables, cereals, and meats such as mutton.

Scotland had poor agricultural land, and climate change made more of it marginal during this period, leaving settlement light, especially in the interior and Highlands. Settlements were farmsteads, some clustered around fortified positions such as brochs, and mixed farming was mostly based on self-sufficiency. Life expectancy was relatively low, and the 5th and 6th centuries likely saw higher mortality from the appearance of bubonic plague, which may have reduced the population.
food.source_title: Scotland in the Early Middle Ages

food.text: Olive oil stayed an expensive import in the north. Oil of poppy, walnut, hazel and filbert was the most affordable alternative for cooks there.

In the law code of King Ine of Wessex, a hide was defined as a unit of land that could be used for collecting food and other goods from the king's subjects. Land was thus measured partly by what it could supply to the crown.

The medieval writer Bede mentions that land in Anglesey and the Isle of Man was divided up in hides. This shows the system of gathering food and goods from the king's subjects reached beyond the Anglo-Saxon heartlands.

A document from the 7th or 8th century, the Tribal Hidage, shows that much of the Anglo-Saxon lands had already been divided into hides by then. Since hides were tied to collecting food and other goods, it hints at how widely the system ran.
Dried figs and dates turned up quite frequently in the north, though cooks used them rather sparingly. They were luxuries carried from far warmer lands.

art.text: A rich artistic culture flourished under the Anglo-Saxons, producing epic poems such as Beowulf and sophisticated metalwork. They also made carved ivories, illuminated manuscripts, embroidered cloths, crosses and stone sculpture, although relatively few of these have survived.

Pictish art was the only uniquely Scottish medieval style. It survives in carved stones, particularly in the north and east of the country, and in elaborate metalwork that largely survives in buried hoards.

Insular art was a common style that developed in Britain and Ireland from the eighth century and became highly influential in continental Europe. It appears in elaborate jewellery, heavily carved high crosses and illustrated manuscripts such as the Book of Kells, which may have been begun, or wholly created, at Iona.

Romanesque architecture developed in parts of France in the 10th century, before the later influence of the Abbey of Cluny. Called "First Romanesque" or "Lombard Romanesque", it is characterised by thick walls, lack of sculpture and rhythmic ornamental arches known as a Lombard band.
Anglo-Saxon metalworkers frequently used gold and garnets. Brooches, buckles, sword hilts and drinking horns were particularly favoured designs.

Irish-Scots art from the kingdom of Dál Riata suggests it was one of the places, as a crossroads between cultures, where the Insular style developed. After Christianisation in the seventh century, artistic styles in Northumbria interacted with those in Ireland and Scotland to form what historians call Insular or Hiberno-Saxon art.
The intricately carved whalebone Franks Casket is thought to have been produced in Northumbria in the early eighth century. It combines pagan, classical and Christian motifs.
The excavated foundations of the 10th-century cathedral at Winchester are marked on the grass of the cathedral close. When built, it was the largest church in northern Europe.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: Early Anglo-Saxon designs, such as those found at the Sutton Hoo burial, used a zoomorphic style heavily influenced by Germanic fashions. Animal shapes were distorted into flowing forms and positioned alongside geometric patterns.

From the 7th century onwards, more naturalistic designs became popular in England, showing a plasticity of form and incorporating both animals and people. In the 10th century, Carolingian styles inspired by Classical imagery entered from the continent and were widely used in the reformed Benedictine monasteries of the south and east.

At Ripon, the cathedral retains an early Anglo-Saxon crypt of c. 670, described as the only substantial Anglo-Saxon element in an English cathedral. A similar crypt survives below the former cathedral of Hexham Abbey.
art.source_title: Architecture of the medieval cathedrals of England

art.text: Scotland has only one known pagan burial, at Dalmeny, Midlothian. It contained a necklace of beads similar to those found in mid-seventh-century southern England, and a gold object from Dalmeny with filigree and garnet resembles sword harness mounts found at Sutton Hoo.

war.text: In 937 King Æthelstan of England fought an alliance of Olaf Guthfrithson, King of Dublin, Constantine II, King of Scotland, and Owain, King of Strathclyde, at the Battle of Brunanburh. The battle lasted all day, and Æthelstan's army pursued the broken alliance until nightfall, slaying great numbers of enemy troops. Five kings and seven earls from Olaf's army were among the dead, and the Annals of Ulster record that several thousands of Norsemen fell. Constantine lost his son, and two of Æthelstan's cousins, Ælfwine and Æthelwine, died on the English side.

The first recorded Viking raid on Ireland came in 795, when Vikings, possibly from Norway, looted the island of Lambay. It began two hundred years of intermittent warfare, with waves of raiders plundering monasteries and towns throughout Ireland. Over those centuries the Vikings established fortified ports at Dublin, Wexford, Waterford, Cork and Limerick, which became the first large towns in Ireland.

Anglo-Saxon armies were built around well-armed noblemen and their households, backed by temporary troops called the fyrd. By the 9th century armies of 20,000 men could be called up, with another 28,000 available to guard urban defences.
Offa of Mercia built a massive defensive dyke to help defend key frontiers. Mercia and the other kingdoms, led by warrior elites, kept competing for territory throughout the 8th century.

Alfred the Great took London from the Danes in 886 and took the title King of the Anglo-Saxons. In 927 his grandson Æthelstan conquered York, the last Viking kingdom. This made him the first Anglo-Saxon ruler of the whole of England.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle poem on Brunanburh says there had never yet been as many people killed with sword's edge since the east Angles and Saxons came over the broad sea. The 937 battle is mentioned in over forty medieval texts.
Under King Penda in the 7th century, Mercia invaded neighbouring lands. It came to loosely control around 50 regiones covering much of England.

Most Anglo-Saxon soldiers fought with spears, while swords were used by wealthier nobles. Cavalry was probably less common than in wider Europe. Viking attacks in the 9th century led to tactical developments, including the use of shield walls in battle.

Ireland had more than 150 different kingdoms ruling small territories. Defeated kings were easily replaced, so it was almost impossible for the Vikings to win control there. The same Viking method of removing a small ruling class had worked against centralised kingdoms elsewhere in Europe.

In 934 Æthelstan invaded Scotland with a large military and naval force. His army harassed the Scots as far as Kincardineshire and his navy went as far as Caithness, but his force was never engaged. John of Worcester said the cause was Constantine's violation of the peace treaty made in 927.

Æthelweard's Chronicon, from around 980, says the battle at Brunandune was still called "the great war". He also says no enemy fleet had attacked the country since. The battle is generally agreed to have been fought at Bromborough on the Wirral.

literature.text: The Anglo-Saxons produced extensive poetry in Old English, some of it written down as early as the 9th century. Beowulf, probably written between 650 and 750, tells a vivid heroic tale that ends with the hero's death at the hands of a dragon. It still shows signs of new Christian influences.
The Anglo-Saxons produced extensive poetry in Old English. Some of it was written down as early as the 9th century, although most surviving poems were compiled in the 10th and early 11th century.

Beowulf, probably written between 650 and 750, portrays a vivid, heroic tale that ends with the hero's death at the hands of a dragon. It still shows signs of the new Christian influences in England, and is typical of the poetry produced by the Anglo-Saxons.

The Canticle of Saint Eulalie, written in the second half of the ninth century, is generally accepted as the first literary text in Old French. It is a short poem that recounts the martyrdom of a young girl. The first literary works in Old French were saints' lives.

Old English literature includes epic poetry, hagiography, sermons, Bible translations, legal works, chronicles and riddles. About 400 manuscripts survive from the period, which ran from the Saxon settlement around 450 until soon after the Norman Conquest in 1066.

Widsith appears in the Exeter Book of the late 10th century and lists the kings of tribes, with Attila King of the Huns first, followed by Eormanric of the Ostrogoths. It may be the oldest surviving work telling the Battle of the Goths and Huns.

Classical antiquity was not forgotten in Anglo-Saxon England. King Alfred's 9th-century translation of Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy is the longest of several Old English poems adapted from late classical philosophical texts.

European debate poetry first appeared in the eighth and ninth centuries, during the Carolingian Renaissance. The first example we have is Conflictus Veris et Hiemis, the Contention of Spring and Winter, written in the late eighth century and commonly attributed to Alcuin.

Lotte Hedeager argues that Widsith is far older than the 10th century and likely dates to the late 6th or early 7th century, citing the author's accurate historical details. She notes that some scholars, such as John Niles, have argued it was invented in the 10th century.
Bede wrote his Ecclesiastical History of the English People in Latin in about AD 731. It was later translated into Old English, sometime between the end of the ninth century and about 930.
tags: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

literature.text: From the 9th century onwards, Old English was also used for academic and courtly writing. This included translations of popular foreign works, such as The Pastoral Care.

The Conflictus Veris et Hiemis set the pattern for later debate poems. It is light hearted but slightly academic, its exchanges are few but succinct, the debate is carefully balanced, and the issue at hand is resolved.

The Canu Heledd poems lament the demise of Cynddylan, king of Pengwern, and name sites from Shropshire to Dogfeiling to Newtown. Their geography probably reflects the time of composition, around the ninth or tenth century, rather than Cynddylan's own seventh-century time.
literature.source_title: Wales in the Early Middle Ages

literature.text: The Old English poem Widsith lists kings of tribes, with Attila King of the Huns first and Eormanric of the Ostrogoths second. It may be the oldest work telling of the Battle of the Goths and Huns, later told in Scandinavian works such as Hervarar's saga and Gesta Danorum.

science.text: Bald's Leechbook is a medical text in Old English and Medieval Latin, probably compiled in the mid-tenth century. Its name has nothing to do with leeches. It comes from the Old English word for a 'book of medical prescriptions'.

The Northumbrian monk Bede wrote The Reckoning of Time in 725. It describes the principal ancient calendars, including those of the Hebrews, Egyptians, Romans, Greeks and Anglo-Saxons. Its main focus was calculating the date of Easter.

Alcuin of York, a leading scholar at Charlemagne's court, wrote on subjects ranging from grammar and biblical exegesis to arithmetic and astronomy. He also collected rare books, which formed the nucleus of the library at York Cathedral.

Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II, is said to have reintroduced the abacus, the armillary sphere and the water organ to Western Christendom. These had been lost to Latin Europe since the fall of the Western Roman Empire. He is also said to be the first in Christian Europe, outside Al-Andalus, to introduce the Hindu-Arabic decimal numerals.

A Latin verse at the end of the Leechbook's second book says, 'Bald owns this book which he ordered Cild to compile.' The book is named after its owner, Bald. The whole text survives in only one manuscript, now in the British Library in London.

In The Reckoning of Time, Bede described the Easter method developed by Dionysius Exiguus. He also gave instructions for calculating the date of the Easter full moon and the motion of the Sun and Moon through the zodiac.
Bede, a Northumbrian monk, studied computus, the science of calculating calendar dates. One of the most important dates he tried to compute was Easter, an effort mired in controversy.

One scholar says Bald's Leechbook shows a conscious effort to bring into Anglo-Saxon practice what one physician thought most useful in native and Mediterranean medicine. Leechbook III, by contrast, reflects Anglo-Saxon medical practice while it was still relatively free of Mediterranean influences. The Lacnunga is described as a commonplace book that simply records medical items.

In mid-7th-century Anglo-Saxon England, there was a desire to tie Easter less closely to the Jewish Passover calendar and to have it observed on a Sunday. This pressure formed the background to Bede's later calendar work in The Reckoning of Time.

Gerbert learned mathematics and astronomy under Bishop Atto of Vich, in Catalan monasteries holding manuscripts from Muslim Spain, especially Córdoba. His student Richer, a monk in Rheims, described how Gerbert used the armillary sphere as a visual aid in the classroom. Richer also stated that Gerbert discovered that stars coursed obliquely across the night sky.

In Old English medical texts, elves were believed to afflict humans and livestock with illnesses, apparently mostly sharp, internal pains and mental disorders. Continental Scandinavia and Iceland also have a scattering of mentions of elves in medical texts, sometimes in the form of amulets, where elves are viewed as a possible cause of illness.

The manuscript holding Bald's Leechbook, Royal 12 D. xvii, was written by the scribe who entered the annals for 925 to 955 into the Parker Chronicle. Those annals were probably produced in Winchester, so the medical manuscript was presumably made there too.

politics.text: In 927, King Æthelstan became the first king to rule a single united Kingdom of England. Wessex, the royal family that opposed the Vikings from the south, had gradually become the dominant power. After his death, however, the Danish settlers and other Anglo-Saxon kingdoms reasserted themselves.

Cnut the Great ruled England, Denmark and Norway together in what is called the North Sea Empire. At the height of his power, from 1028 to 1035, he was the most powerful ruler in western Europe after the Holy Roman Emperor. His realm was held together only by the sea.

In 865 the Danish micel here, or Great Army, invaded England, captured York and defeated the kingdom of East Anglia. Mercia and Northumbria fell in 875 and 876. Alfred of Wessex was driven into internal exile in 878.

France in the Middle Ages was a decentralised, feudal monarchy. In regions such as Brittany, Normandy and Aquitaine, the authority of the French king was barely felt. The kingdom evolved from the fragmentation of West Francia (843 to 987) to gradual centralisation under the House of Capet, which began in 987.

Offa of Mercia, who reigned from 757 to 796, is remembered for building the 150-mile-long Offa's Dyke. It formed the Wales/England border, though it is not clear whether it was a boundary line or a defensive position. His reign was the climax of Mercia's long conflict with the Welsh kingdom of Powys.

The kingdom of Wessex developed a centralised royal administration. Its king's council, the witenagemot, comprised senior clergy, ealdormen and important thegns, and advised the king on policy and legal issues. The post of sheriff emerged in the 10th century to administer local shires on behalf of an ealdorman.

Hywel Dda, king of Deheubarth, came close to uniting Wales. In 942 he intervened when Idwal Foel of Gwynedd was defeated in battle by Edmund, King of England, and took control of Gwynedd and Powys. He instituted Welsh law, which was adopted across Wales even after his kingdom was divided after his death.
politics.source_title: Wales in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: In the 9th century, the House of Alpin combined the lands of the Scots and Picts to form a single kingdom. This became the basis of the Kingdom of Scotland. Viking pressure may have speeded the process: after raids began in 793, the king of Fortriu and the king of Dál Riata were among the dead after a major defeat by the Vikings in 839, and in 870 the Vikings stormed the Briton fortress of Dumbarton. Before that, four kingdoms had been the most important: the Picts, the Gaels of Dál Riata, the Britons of Alt Clut, and the Anglian kingdom of Bernicia.
politics.source_title: Scotland in the Early Middle Ages

politics.text: Cnut's coins suggest how he presented his power. Some were inscribed CNVT REX SW, meaning Cnut King of the Swedes, and he also had coins minted proclaiming him ruler of Ireland. The inscription may have been propaganda or boasting, since Cnut did not need to be present in Sweden for them to be produced.

Cnut proclaimed his son Harthacnut king of Denmark at a great court in Nidaros. By appointing different sons as heirs in different countries, he showed he did not intend an empire that would remain united after his death. The weakness of his empire was the impossibility of finding loyal and competent regents when he could not be present.

In France between the late 9th and late 10th centuries, the aristocracy focused on taking hereditary control of counties and duchies. They eventually turned these into virtually independent principalities and privatised rights of the state. By 1025, the area north of the Loire was dominated by six or seven of these states.

Anglo-Saxon kings kept tight control over the mints, which provided a high-quality currency. The whole country was taxed using a system called hidage. Under the Danish kings, a bodyguard of housecarls also accompanied the court.

philosophy.text: Medieval philosophy as a project of independent inquiry began in Baghdad in the middle of the 8th century. In France and Germany it began in the last quarter of the 8th century, in the itinerant court of Charlemagne at Aachen.

Charlemagne, advised by Candidus, Peter of Pisa and Alcuin of York, attracted the scholars of England and Ireland. By imperial decree in 787 he established schools in every abbey in his empire. These schools gave Scholasticism its name and became centres of medieval learning.

Johannes Scotus Eriugena (c. 815 to 877) was an Irish theologian and Neoplatonic philosopher who succeeded Alcuin of York as head of the Palace School. He translated and wrote commentaries on the work of Pseudo-Dionysius, which was initially thought to be from the apostolic age.

At Fleury, Theodulphus, bishop of Orléans, established a school for young noblemen recommended there by Charlemagne. By the mid-ninth century its library was one of the most comprehensive ever assembled in the West.

Paulinus founded a school and a minster at York in the early seventh century, and the School at York Minster is one of the oldest in England. By the late eighth century its library was estimated at one hundred volumes. Alcuin was a student and teacher there before leaving for Charlemagne's court in 782.

Catharism was a movement with Gnostic elements that originated around the middle of the 10th century, in Languedoc and the surrounding areas of southern France. The contemporary Roman Catholic Church branded it heretical. The article says these heresies were on a scale the Church had never seen before, and that its response was one of elimination for some of them, the Cathars among them.

Knowledge of Ancient Greek had vanished in the West except in Ireland, where it was fairly common in monastic schools. Irish scholars were renowned for their learning at the Frankish court. Johannes Scotus Eriugena translated many works into Latin, giving access to the Cappadocian Fathers and the Greek theological tradition.
Around Eriugena's time a controversy arose over whether God had predestined some people for salvation and some for damnation. Eriugena was called in to settle the dispute.

Paschasius Radbertus raised a question about the real presence of Christ at the Eucharist: how can the host be present in many places and times? He argued that Christ's real body is present, veiled by the appearance of bread and wine, at all places and times through God's incomprehensible power.

The Viking attack on Lindisfarne in 793 was a catastrophic blow and the first of many raids on the monasteries of Northumbria. The Lindisfarne Gospels survived, but monastic culture went into decline in the early ninth century, and repeated Viking assaults on religious centres were one reason for the drop in manuscript production. The devastating raid on Lindisfarne marked the beginning of a century of Viking invasions that severely limited the production and survival of Anglo-Saxon material culture.
Johannes Scotus Eriugena, who lived from 815 to 877, was the most significant Irish intellectual of the early monastic period. He was regarded as an outstanding philosopher in terms of originality.

Johannes Scotus Eriugena, an Irish theologian and Neoplatonic philosopher, succeeded Alcuin of York as head of the Palace School. He translated and commented on the work of Pseudo-Dionysius, and was called in to settle a dispute over whether God had predestined some for salvation and some for damnation.

Scholars such as Lupus of Ferrières, who died in 862, traveled to Fleury to consult its texts. Later, under St. Abbo of Fleury, abbot from 988 to 1004, the reformed abbey school enjoyed a second golden age.

Paschasius Radbertus raised the question of Christ's real presence at the Eucharist. He argued that Christ's real body is present, veiled by the appearance of bread and wine, and is present at all places and all times by means of God's incomprehensible power.

culture.text: When Roman authority collapsed, formal Christianity ended in the east of what is now England, as Germanic settlers established paganism across the lands they controlled. Pope Gregory I later sent missionaries, and most Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were converted. The process was largely complete by the end of the seventh century.

Pope Gregory I sent missionaries who gradually converted most of the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms, while Scots-Irish monks were active in the north. The process was largely complete by the end of the seventh century. It left a confusing and disparate array of local practices and religious ceremonies.

Pope Gregory I sent a team of missionaries, known as the Gregorian mission, to convert King Æthelberht of Kent and his household. Augustine became the first Archbishop of Canterbury and began building new churches across the South-East. He reused existing pagan shrines for them.

The Franks Casket, believed to have been made in Northumbria in the early eighth century, mixes Germanic legends with stories of the founding of Rome and the Roman Church. It shows that blending pagan and Christian imagery was not unique to the later Danelaw.

The Gosforth Cross, dated to the early tenth century, stands 14 feet (4.4 m) tall and is carved with mythical beasts, Norse gods and Christian symbolism. One side shows the Crucifixion, while the other shows scenes from Ragnarok. Stone sculpture was not a native Scandinavian practice, so such monuments show English influence on Viking settlers.

St. Columba, an Irish monk, left Ireland and founded the monastery at Iona off the west coast of Scotland in 563. From there he carried out missions to the Scots of Dál Riata and the Picts. The article describes both Columba and the Irish missionary Saint Kessog, who founded his abbey about 490, as martyrs.
culture.source_title: Scotland in the Early Middle Ages

culture.text: Anglo-Saxon Christianity reflected the military culture of the Anglo-Saxons. As kings converted in the sixth and seventh centuries, conversion was used as a justification for war against the remaining pagan kingdoms. Christian saints were also imbued with martial properties.

By the 10th century the parish system was well established in England, and parish priests were typically local men with a basic education. Many were married, especially in the North, though priestly celibacy was becoming more common. For the literate there was plenty of religious writing in English, such as the Blickling homilies and the writings of Ælfric.

In the early Middle Ages, church music in Britain was dominated by monophonic plainchant. Because British Christianity developed separately from Rome's direct influence until the eighth century, a distinct form of liturgical Celtic chant emerged. No notations of it survive, though later sources suggest distinctive melodic patterns.

In Wales, everyone from ruler down to slave was defined by their kindred family, the tud, and their individual status, the braint. Wales was rural throughout the era, with small settlements called trefi, controlled by a warrior aristocracy who held the land and, by extension, the people on it. Many of those people were tenant peasants or slaves, answerable to the aristocrat who controlled their land. Slaves sat at the bottom of society and could form part of a payment between those of higher rank; hereditary slavery was more common than penal slavery, though some could buy their freedom. There was no sense of a coherent tribe of people.
culture.source_title: Wales in the Early Middle Ages

culture.text: On the Gosforth Cross, Mary Magdalene is depicted as a valkyrie, with a trailing dress and long pigtail. This may mean the Vikings initially accepted the Christian god as an addition to their many pagan gods, rather than a replacement.
